title: KV cache architecture & eviction/paging deep dive - Aurora Data Systems
summary: Deep technical session focused on KV cache architecture and troubleshooting for long-context workloads: eviction behavior, paging, prefix reuse, and interactions with batching/quantization. Discussed root causes of unexpected evictions, mitigations (pinning, tombstones, cache-aware batching), on-prem/VPC implications, and next steps to run benchmarks and share tuning docs.
transcript:
Meeting header:
Date: 2026-12-07
Start: 15:00 PT
Duration: ~64 minutes
Attendees: Maya (Redwood AE), Liam (Redwood SE), Jordan (Redwood SE), Priya (Aurora), Eliot (Aurora Security), Noah (Aurora ML)

Summary (auto): brief -- KV cache evictions happening when sessions extend beyond 8k tokens; paging observed causing 100-300ms p99 spikes; prefix reuse causing cache fragmentation. Action: run targeted bench with pinned prefixes + page_size tweak; Redwood to share tuning guide + benchmark sheet.

00:00 Maya (AE): hey everyone thanks for joining on such short notice, uh we pulled in Liam and Jordan from the SE team to do a deep dive on the KV stuff you flagged last week, Priya can you quickly recap what you're seeing?
00:18 Priya: yeah thanks, so we've got prod traffic with long multi-turn sessions, sometimes up to 40k tokens, and we're seeing steady increases in token latency after about 12 minutes per session. It manifests as periodic 150 to 300 ms p99 jumps and then larger stalls when pages are flushed.
00:34 Eliot: to add, we correlate with increased cache miss rate in our dashboards, and eviction counts spike right before the latency increases. We've tried bumping instance size but didn't fully eliminate it.
00:47 Liam (SE): okay that's helpful; quick clarification — you said 40k context, is that cumulative across turns or contiguous?
00:53 Noah: it's contiguous, we stream earlier conversation as part of the prompt, so KV grows basically with each turn until we prune.
01:02 Jordan (SE): cool, so two main things to watch — absolute KV size vs configured cache capacity, and prefix reuse behavior. When similar prefixes are used repeatedly we expect reuse, but if prefixes are slightly different (tokenization drift, metadata tokens), that causes near-duplicates and cache fragmentation which increases memory pressure.
01:21 Sara (Security): before we dive too deep — from a security standpoint we need to ensure any pinning or caching behavior doesn't leak across tenants; we're on VPC private deployment so keys live in our KMS but we want confirmation on per-tenant isolation.
01:34 Liam: absolutely — with Redwood Private each customer KV is namespaced per session/customer and encryption at rest is handled by your KMS/HSM. We'll attach the security whitepaper after the call, but Jordan will detail the per-tenant isolation model in a minute.
01:47 Jordan: quick architecture sketch — KV is an LRU-approx structure split into pages. Each page holds N key-value entries; eviction happens at page-level when memory threshold is hit. We do an MRU window for hot prefixes to avoid thrashing, but if new unique prefixes arrive quickly you'll see page churn.
02:10 Priya: is the page granularity tunable? we thought we were on a default 4MB page and guessed that might be too coarse for our workload with many small prefixes.
02:21 Jordan: yes page_size and page_count are configurable in Dedicated/Private. Smaller page_size reduces internal fragmentation but increases management overhead and slightly higher CPU, because more pages = more meta bookkeeping. For your profile — lots of small distinct prefixes — smaller pages are usually better.
02:40 Noah: what's the tradeoff on latency for smaller pages? we can't accept additional p99 regressions.
02:46 Liam: good question — in practice page-level ops are async and we only see a small CPU bump on host, so token generation latency is usually unaffected if you size the host appropriately. The main cost is memory efficiency. If you go from 4MB to 1MB pages you reduce wasted slots and cut eviction churn, which should reduce the spikes you're seeing.
03:05 Eliot: we've also seen something that looks like prefix reuse failing — same prompt id but different session metadata gets a new entry. Is there deduping or canonicalization we can enable?
03:15 Jordan: yes there's a prefix-canonicalization pipeline that normalizes whitespace and some metadata tokens; but it won't canonicalize semantically different embeddings. If your pipeline injects per-request trace ids into the prompt, that will negate reuse — make sure trace ids are outside the prefix hashed region or sent as metadata headers.
03:33 Priya: hmm we do include request ids inside the prompt for debugging, could be the root cause. We'll try moving those out.
03:40 Sara: also from security — if you move trace ids to headers we need SSO/SAML integration to still map requests back to sessions for audit.
03:48 Maya: noted, we'll include an integration note.
03:52 Liam: another behavior to call out — eviction can be exacerbated by batching. If you batch a lot of requests with different prefixes, the runtime will prefetch many KV pages into GPU memory and if those prefixes aren't later reused you'll cause churn. For cost/latency you usually want workload-aware batching: group by prefix or session when possible.
04:14 Noah: what's the recommended batch size for long-context? we're currently pushing 32 variable-length requests per batch.
04:21 Jordan: grouping by prefix is more important than a fixed batch size; if you can't group, reduce variable-concurrency so you don't prefetch unrelated prefixes. For long-context you can set batching policy to session-affinity: it keeps batches to same session until partial completion. That mitigates prefetch storms.
04:40 Eliot: we also ran quantized models to save memory — have you seen interactions between quantization (int8/4) and KV behavior?
04:46 Liam: yes, quantization affects model memory but KV is separate; however, lower model memory sometimes leads teams to pack more concurrent sessions on the same host which increases aggregate KV resident set. Also quantized kernels may change timing so prefetch heuristics occasionally misfire; we have heuristics tuned per quant profile in Redwood Optimize.
05:08 Priya: can we pin hot prefixes so they're never evicted?
05:11 Jordan: yes — pinning is supported but should be used carefully. Pinning creates permanent entries and can push other important prefixes out; we recommend pin the top 1-2% hottest prefixes only and monitor eviction pressure. We also support TTLs per pinned item so you can auto-unpin after stable period.
05:33 Noah: what's the observable to pick top hot prefixes?
05:36 Liam: the Console shows top-k prefix hit rate and eviction counters per prefix hash. You'll see a small table and a CSV download link. We'll share an example query.
05:44 Priya: can you explain the "tombstone" concept you mentioned last time? we saw tombstone entries in the logs.
05:49 Jordan: tombstones are markers we leave after deletion to avoid immediate re-insert thrash; if you aggressively delete and re-insert the same key you'd otherwise oscillate. Tombstones have a short TTL and are auto-compacted. Too many tombstones means frequent churn — usually a symptom of upstream churn (clients rewriting prefixes or rotating metadata).
06:12 Eliot: we do rotate user metadata tokens at every API call for compliance — could that be creating tombstones?
06:18 Jordan: yes that pattern will create churn; best practice is separate immutable prefix (the conversational history) from ephemeral metadata token. Put ephemeral tokens in headers if possible.
06:24 Priya: can you run through the recommended debugging bench you'd like us to run? concrete steps would be great.
06:30 Liam: sure — two runs: 1) synthetic long-context run that increments session length to 40k tokens with constant prefix canonicalization disabled (to reproduce), and 2) the same with trace ids moved out + page_size reduced to 1MB + pin top 1% prefixes. Collect metrics: eviction_count, tombstone_rate, page_faults, prefetch_count, and latency p50/p95/p99. We'll give you the bench harness and expected config.
06:58 Jordan: also capture heap and GPU resident KV mem snapshots every minute; we have a script to interpret those. We'll attach it.
07:07 Priya: timing — when can we get the harness?
07:10 Maya: we'll email the harness and config today; Jordan will own the bench sheet and Liam will help run an initial trial next week.
07:18 Sara: on the audit side we need to confirm that pinned prefixes don't change retention policies and that audit logs still capture who pinned/unpinned.
07:25 Jordan: audit events for cache ops are in the Console logs for Private by default; we can increase retention for pinned events as an add-on. I'll note that in the action items.
07:36 Eliot: one more weird observation — we see paging I/O to local SSD on Private when memory spikes; is that normal?
07:42 Liam: yes, paging is a design where we spill cold pages to local NVMe to avoid full eviction across sessions; but I/O spikes mean your page_size/pages count mismatch or your disk bandwidth is starved. We can tune the spill threshold or increase local SSD bandwidth. If you're in cloud t2-style instances, NVMe is slower; pick instances with better local disk throughput for heavy paging workloads.
08:05 Noah: performance numbers — what's a typical p99 impact of page spill vs full eviction?
08:10 Jordan: page spill usually adds 20-80ms depending on SSD. Full eviction and reload can add 150-400ms depending on host and GPU memory sync.
08:20 Priya: that matches what we saw.
08:23 Maya: high level recs so far: canonicalize prefixes (move trace ids), reduce page_size to 1MB for your small-prefix profile, enable session-affinity batching, pin top 1% hot prefixes with TTL, increase NVMe throughput or raise spill threshold, and run bench. We'll send a config diff.
08:39 Sara: any compliance notes on moving trace ids to headers? they contain PII sometimes.
08:44 Jordan: headers are still within the same request boundary and encrypted in transit; for audit we can log hashes instead of cleartext and map them in your secure environment. We'll include guidance.
08:58 Priya: one more — can Redwood run an internal sim on your side to replicate, or do we need to run it here?
09:04 Liam: we can replicate a best-effort sim in Redwood Dedicated infra but for exact parity we prefer you run in Private since KMS and instance types differ. We'll run a complementary sim and compare results.
09:16 Maya: okay let's capture next steps and owners.
09:20 [short pause, note of shared links: KV tuning guide: https://redwood.example.com/kv-tuning, bench sheet: https://redwood.example.com/benchmarks/aurora-kv, audit whitepaper link] 
09:35 Action recap and next steps:
09:38 Maya: Jordan — share KV tuning guide + bench harness + heap snapshot script (today).
09:44 Jordan: will do.
09:46 Maya: Liam — help run initial bench and join customer-run trial next Wed (2026-12-15).
09:52 Liam: yes, I'll be there.
09:54 Priya: Aurora will move trace ids out, run bench with the two configs, and share results.
10:00 Priya: we'll try pin top prefixes and reduce page_size and report back.
10:05 Maya: any other Qs?
10:07 Sara: when you share the security docs can you highlight the audit entries for pin/unpin and KMS integration?
10:12 Jordan: yes, will annotate the whitepaper.
10:15 Maya: great thanks everyone, we'll follow up by EOD with the artifacts and schedule.
10:20 End of recording.

Notes: transcription has minor mis-labels; timestamps approximate. Some technical terms slightly garbled in spots (example: "prefetch storms" sometimes transcribed as "prefetch storms" vs "prefetch storms" same).
